problem: The caption says 'only the indirect route removes sliding between billet and container wall'. Section 3 says hydrostatic extrusion has no container friction because a fluid film separates billet and container. A student reading only the caption will think hydrostatic extrusion still has direct wall friction like the direct route.
fix: Say: 'indirect removes billet–container friction because the billet does not move relative to the container; hydrostatic also removes it, by floating the billet on a pressurised fluid film.'

problem: Toothpaste tubes are listed with aluminium window sections, heat-sink fins and ladder rails as products that 'come out as one long continuous piece'. Tubes are not continuous lengths; they are single impact-extruded cups, as Section 3 itself explains.
fix: Keep the continuous-length examples for die extrusion and mention toothpaste tubes separately: '...ladder rails are made this way; toothpaste tubes and aerosol cans are made by a one-blow variant, impact extrusion (Section 3).'

problem: 'volume conservation forces a long thin wall' is vague and does not say what sets thickness and what sets length, so a student may still think a longer punch stroke gives a thinner wall.
fix: Write: 'The wall thickness is fixed by the annular gap between punch and die (typically well under 1 mm). The punch stroke fixes the length of the cup, because the slug volume is conserved: slug volume = cup base + wall volume. Thickness and stroke are therefore independent.'
